40	The header is frozen. rb_insert returns −1 and
41	the caller still owns the value.
42	Overwriting frees the old value
43	through value_free, and
44	nobody else does.
45	
46	Required operations: rb_create, rb_insert (with rebalancing), rb_find, rb_delete
47	(with the full deletion-fixup cases; yes, all of them), rb_size, rb_foreach (in-order), rb_validate,
48	rb_destroy.
49	
50	rb_validate must check, and your tests must exercise, all invariants (Section 3, Figure 1):
51	1. The root is black.
52	2. No red node has a red child.
53	3. Every root-to-NIL path contains the same number b of black nodes (the tree’s black-height); so
54	the tree height is O(log n).
55	4. In-order traversal yields strictly increasing keys: k1 < k2 < · · · < kn under strcmp.
56	5. rb_size matches the actual node count n
57	
58	you must also write table-driven tests for rb_delete covering, at minimum: a red leaf, a
59	black leaf with a red sibling, a node with two children, and deletion of the root. Each test asserts
60	rb_validate and rb_size afterward.
61	
62	Memory rules: rb_destroy must free every node together with its key copy and, when a
63	destructor was supplied, every value as well; both verification builds must come back with zero
64	findings across your entire suite, empty tree included, because you tested the empty tree. Recursion
65	is permitted this time, in rb_destroy and rb_foreach alike. Savor that. The next assignment
66	revokes it, and Section 10 lets you find out early what the revocation costs.
67	
68	Route all allocation in src/rbtree.c through two four line wrappers. rb_malloc and rb_free, that simply forward to malloc and free. 
69	
70	you will be required to tear down a
71	million-node tree in O(1) auxiliary space: no recursion, no heap-allocated stack, a couple of local
72	variables and nothing more.
73	The classic trick is lovely. As you free, rotate the tree into a right spine, so there is never a left
74	subtree left to remember; the tree’s own pointer fields become the bookkeeping. If you want a head
75	start on next month, implement it now behind a second function and check it against your fuzzer’s
76	teardown. 
77	
78	plan first, keep the diffs small, verify everything with tools, and merge
79	nothing the user cannot explain.
80	
81	rb_validate must show a failure reason when it breaks a rule.
82	
83	 fixup must never dereference memory that has already been freed.
84	
85	account for the deletion case of deleting a black node with exactly one child. 
86	
87	**Thresholds**: 
88	your fuzzer (tests/fuzz.c) performs ≥ 10^5
89	random insert/find/delete operations against a reference model (a sorted array or a simple linked list is fine), calling rb_validate
90	at least every 100 operations, under both asan and memcheck.
91	
92	**Choices left to me**: 
93	
94	We will add the optional seam, rb_malloc and rb_free (routing as seen in contracts)
95	
96	I would like to add a parent pointer. 
97	
98	The mirror image (a right child of a right child, needing a left rotation at the grandparent) is
99	the same code with left and right swapped, and it is the half people forget. Do not forget it.
100	And it is worth handing this exact sequence to Claude Code in plan mode, asking it to predict each
101	panel before you scroll, because arguing about 35 for ten minutes now is considerably cheaper than
102	discovering at the walkthrough that you learned deletion fixup and merely memorized this.
103	FIGURE 4
104	
105	We decided to extend the fuzzer to include case 3, where we need an extended fixup to climb up the tree. There was a gap in coverage. This also was to cover the fact that the 9 table-driven cases we came up with did not exercse a multi-level delete_fixup climb (case 3 recoloring and moving up more than one ancestor) or a debt that climbs up to the root. 
106	
107	
108	
109	
110	
111	**Confusions:**
112	
113	Deletion case key (study aid, from quizzing myself against spec Section 3, pages 11-16
114	— rb_delete isn't implemented yet, this is the decision tree to code against):
115	
116	Every deletion, no matter how it starts, reduces to "unlink a node with at most one child."
117	
118	STEP 0 — reduce to the base case:
119	  - if the node to delete has two children:
120	      find its in-order successor Y (leftmost node in its right subtree),
121	      copy Y's key/value into the doomed node's slot (the node ITSELF stays in the
122	      tree, keeps its own color/pointers — only key/value move),
123	      then delete Y instead. Y is guaranteed to have at most one child
124	      (it's the leftmost node in a subtree, so no left child).
125	  - now you're always unlinking some node N with 0 or 1 children.
126	
127	STEP 1 — what color is N?
128	  if N is RED:
129	      -> N must be a leaf (a red node's children are NIL/black-only, and if N had
130	         one child that child would be black, which would already break black-height
131	         before you touched anything — so a red N can't have exactly one child).
132	      -> unlink and free it. No fixup. Black-height on that path never changes.
133	      -> DONE. (Case 1: red leaf.)
134	
135	  if N is BLACK and has exactly one child C:
136	      -> C must be RED (same black-height argument, mirrored: a black child there
137	         would already have broken invariant 3 before deletion).
138	      -> splice C into N's slot, paint C black, free N.
139	      -> C now carries exactly the black N used to carry. No debt created.
140	      -> DONE, no sibling-based fixup loop should run. (Case 6, Figure 8 — the
141	         "side door" case that two-children reduction walks into constantly.)
142	
143	  if N is BLACK and has zero children (a black leaf):
144	      -> the slot left behind is "doubly black" (owes one black node). This is
145	         the only case that needs the real fixup loop. Go to STEP 2.
146	
147	STEP 2 — doubly-black fixup loop (only reached for: black leaf, no children).
148	  Look at the doubly-black slot's SIBLING (S) and PARENT (P).
149	
150	  if S is RED:
151	      -> (forces P black, S's children black, by rule 4/5).
152	      -> rotate S up over P, swap colors (P <-> S's old color).
153	      -> NOTHING is fixed yet — this is a pure reshuffle, no black-height changed
154	         anywhere (you rotated a red node, which is free, and only swapped colors
155	         1-for-1 between P and S).
156	      -> new sibling is now guaranteed BLACK (was S's own child).
157	      -> re-run STEP 2 from the top with the new sibling. (Case 5.)
158	
159	  if S is BLACK and has at least one RED child:
160	      -> recoloring is illegal here (painting S red would stack it under its own
161	         red child = new red-red violation).
162	      -> rotate the red nephew into the deficient side, recolor on arrival so the
163	         relocated red node becomes the missing black.
164	      -> TERMINAL. Debt fully paid in this one step, regardless of P's color.
165	         Never climbs further. (Case 4.)
166	
167	  if S is BLACK and both children are BLACK/NIL:
168	      -> no red material anywhere nearby to rotate with — rotating black nodes
169	         here only moves an existing black around, it can't manufacture a new one.
170	      -> recolor S red (strips a black from S's branch too, so both branches under
171	         P now agree, both one-short) then:
172	         if P is RED: recolor P black. P absorbs the shared debt. DONE. (Case 3a,
173	            the deletion-twin of insert's red-uncle case — 2 recolors, 0 rotations.)
174	         if P is BLACK: nothing absorbs the debt. The doubly-black marker moves up
175	            to P. Re-run STEP 2 with P's slot as the new deficient node. (Case 3b —
176	            this is the case that climbs, possibly to the root.)
177	
178	  if the debt climbs all the way to the root: it just disappears — a root with
179	  no black debt above it needs nothing further, black-height simply dropped by one
180	  uniformly, which is legal (invariant 3 only requires paths to AGREE, not a fixed
181	  absolute count).
182	
183	Mirror image reminder: every "left/right" in the above has a mirror where sibling
184	hangs off the other side. Do not forget it — same bug shape as insert fixup's
185	LR/RL mirror, and the spec calls it "the half people forget" a second time here.
186	
187	Memory-safety trap specific to this loop: N (the physically unlinked node) is often
188	freed BEFORE the fixup loop runs (fixup only needs P/S/N's old position, not N
189	itself). If N is freed early, save whatever pointers the fixup loop needs (P, S,
190	N's parent slot) before the free, not after — same rule as the single-child splice
191	case, just spread across a whole loop instead of one splice.
192	
193	**Errors Caught**
194	
195	**Personal Notes**
196	We did not use a shared sentinel due to how every parent with a missing child would claim that that one shared sentinel is their child, when in reality the parent which most recently wrote to it, is the one who is the parent.
197	
198	We did not decide to update parent pointers during destruction/teardown due to the fact that it will all be destroyed regardless, so there is not benefit to the additional writes. 
199	
200	rb_create can return null when allocation fails. There is no clean up because the only allocation was the failed attempt so there is nothing else to unwind. 
201	
202	You only ever act during insert-fixup if there is a red-red violation
203	 1. if the uncle is red, recolor and run up the tree to the root.
204	 2. if the uncle is black or NIL, rotate. 
205	 2a. If x and parent are left left or right right, rotate at the root.
206	 2b. if x and parent are right left or left right, rotate the parent to straighten a line, then at the grandparent to finsih it. 
207	
208	Invariant 1: Root is red
209	Invariant 2: red-red violation
210	Invariant 3: black height violation
211	
212	
213	
214	
215	The loop invariant (insert_fixup, src/rbtree.c:74-137), at the top of every iteration — i.e., exactly when while (is_red(z->parent)) is checked:
216	
217	1. z is red.
218	2. If z's parent is the root, that parent is black. (Equivalently: whenever the loop body actually runs, z->parent is not the root.)
219	3. Every red-black property that could be violated (no-red-red, equal black-height) has at most one violation in the whole tree, and it is exactly the edge z–z->parent both being red. Everywhere else — including every black-height count — the tree is a legal red-black tree.

teardown.

your fuzzer (tests/fuzz.c) performs ≥ 10^5
random insert/find/delete operations against a reference model (a sorted array or a simple linked list is fine), calling rb_validate
at least every 100 operations, under both asan and memcheck.

I would like to add a parent pointer. 

The mirror image (a right child of a right child, needing a left rotation at the grandparent) is
the same code with left and right swapped, and it is the half people forget. Do not forget it.
And it is worth handing this exact sequence to Claude Code in plan mode, asking it to predict each
panel before you scroll, because arguing about 35 for ten minutes now is considerably cheaper than
discovering at the walkthrough that you learned deletion fixup and merely memorized this.
FIGURE 4

We decided to extend the fuzzer to include case 3, where we need an extended fixup to climb up the tree. There was a gap in coverage. This also was to cover the fact that the 9 table-driven cases we came up with did not exercse a multi-level delete_fixup climb (case 3 recoloring and moving up more than one ancestor) or a debt that climbs up to the root. 





**Confusions:**

Deletion case key (study aid, from quizzing myself against spec Section 3, pages 11-16
— rb_delete isn't implemented yet, this is the decision tree to code against):

Every deletion, no matter how it starts, reduces to "unlink a node with at most one child."

STEP 0 — reduce to the base case:
  - if the node to delete has two children:
      find its in-order successor Y (leftmost node in its right subtree),
      copy Y's key/value into the doomed node's slot (the node ITSELF stays in the
      tree, keeps its own color/pointers — only key/value move),
      then delete Y instead. Y is guaranteed to have at most one child
      (it's the leftmost node in a subtree, so no left child).
  - now you're always unlinking some node N with 0 or 1 children.

STEP 1 — what color is N?
  if N is RED:
      -> N must be a leaf (a red node's children are NIL/black-only, and if N had
         one child that child would be black, which would already break black-height
         before you touched anything — so a red N can't have exactly one child).
      -> unlink and free it. No fixup. Black-height on that path never changes.
      -> DONE. (Case 1: red leaf.)

  if N is BLACK and has exactly one child C:
      -> C must be RED (same black-height argument, mirrored: a black child there
         would already have broken invariant 3 before deletion).
      -> splice C into N's slot, paint C black, free N.
      -> C now carries exactly the black N used to carry. No debt created.
      -> DONE, no sibling-based fixup loop should run. (Case 6, Figure 8 — the
         "side door" case that two-children reduction walks into constantly.)

  if N is BLACK and has zero children (a black leaf):
      -> the slot left behind is "doubly black" (owes one black node). This is
         the only case that needs the real fixup loop. Go to STEP 2.

STEP 2 — doubly-black fixup loop (only reached for: black leaf, no children).
  Look at the doubly-black slot's SIBLING (S) and PARENT (P).

  if S is RED:
      -> (forces P black, S's children black, by rule 4/5).
      -> rotate S up over P, swap colors (P <-> S's old color).
      -> NOTHING is fixed yet — this is a pure reshuffle, no black-height changed
         anywhere (you rotated a red node, which is free, and only swapped colors
         1-for-1 between P and S).
      -> new sibling is now guaranteed BLACK (was S's own child).
      -> re-run STEP 2 from the top with the new sibling. (Case 5.)

  if S is BLACK and has at least one RED child:
      -> recoloring is illegal here (painting S red would stack it under its own
         red child = new red-red violation).
      -> rotate the red nephew into the deficient side, recolor on arrival so the
         relocated red node becomes the missing black.
      -> TERMINAL. Debt fully paid in this one step, regardless of P's color.
         Never climbs further. (Case 4.)

  if S is BLACK and both children are BLACK/NIL:
      -> no red material anywhere nearby to rotate with — rotating black nodes
         here only moves an existing black around, it can't manufacture a new one.
      -> recolor S red (strips a black from S's branch too, so both branches under
         P now agree, both one-short) then:
         if P is RED: recolor P black. P absorbs the shared debt. DONE. (Case 3a,
            the deletion-twin of insert's red-uncle case — 2 recolors, 0 rotations.)
         if P is BLACK: nothing absorbs the debt. The doubly-black marker moves up
            to P. Re-run STEP 2 with P's slot as the new deficient node. (Case 3b —
            this is the case that climbs, possibly to the root.)

  if the debt climbs all the way to the root: it just disappears — a root with
  no black debt above it needs nothing further, black-height simply dropped by one
  uniformly, which is legal (invariant 3 only requires paths to AGREE, not a fixed
  absolute count).

Mirror image reminder: every "left/right" in the above has a mirror where sibling
hangs off the other side. Do not forget it — same bug shape as insert fixup's
LR/RL mirror, and the spec calls it "the half people forget" a second time here.

Memory-safety trap specific to this loop: N (the physically unlinked node) is often
freed BEFORE the fixup loop runs (fixup only needs P/S/N's old position, not N
itself). If N is freed early, save whatever pointers the fixup loop needs (P, S,
N's parent slot) before the free, not after — same rule as the single-child splice
case, just spread across a whole loop instead of one splice.

**Errors Caught**

**Personal Notes**
We did not use a shared sentinel due to how every parent with a missing child would claim that that one shared sentinel is their child, when in reality the parent which most recently wrote to it, is the one who is the parent.

We did not decide to update parent pointers during destruction/teardown due to the fact that it will all be destroyed regardless, so there is not benefit to the additional writes. 

rb_create can return null when allocation fails. There is no clean up because the only allocation was the failed attempt so there is nothing else to unwind. 

You only ever act during insert-fixup if there is a red-red violation
 1. if the uncle is red, recolor and run up the tree to the root.
 2. if the uncle is black or NIL, rotate. 
 2a. If x and parent are left left or right right, rotate at the root.
 2b. if x and parent are right left or left right, rotate the parent to straighten a line, then at the grandparent to finsih it. 

Invariant 1: Root is red
Invariant 2: red-red violation
Invariant 3: black height violation




The loop invariant (insert_fixup, src/rbtree.c:74-137), at the top of every iteration — i.e., exactly when while (is_red(z->parent)) is checked:

1. z is red.
2. If z's parent is the root, that parent is black. (Equivalently: whenever the loop body actually runs, z->parent is not the root.)
3. Every red-black property that could be violated (no-red-red, equal black-height) has at most one violation in the whole tree, and it is exactly the edge z–z->parent both being red. Everywhere else — including every black-height count — the tree is a legal red-black tree.

I've reviewed the deletion-fixup spec section (NOTES.md lines 111–191), the current `delete_fixup`/`rb_delete` implementation (`src/rbtree.c:188–284`), and the table-driven delete tests (`tests/test_rbtree.c:312–426`).

**Finding first:** `rb_delete`/`delete_fixup` are already fully implemented — every case in the spec's decision tree, including both mirrors, is present in the code, and 9 of the required cases are exercised by `delete_cases[]`. So this isn't "write the fixup from scratch" — it's "audit each spec case against the code and the test table, slice by slice, and fill the one documented gap." NOTES.md line 105 explicitly flags that gap: the 9 table-driven cases never exercised a **multi-level Case 3b climb** (recolor-and-move-up more than one ancestor, or a debt that climbs all the way to the root) — that gap was patched in the fuzzer, not in `test_rbtree.c`.

## Plan

**Slice 0 — reduction to base case (STEP 0/1, not the fixup loop itself)**
- Situation: two-children delete (successor splice), red-leaf delete, black-node-with-one-red-child delete. Handled in `rb_delete` (`rbtree.c:246–284`), before `delete_fixup` is ever called.
- Mirror: none needed — successor-splice logic isn't left/right-asymmetric; the one-red-child splice's mirror is data-direction only (left vs right child), already covered by cases below.
- Existing tests: `"delete red leaf"` / `"(mirror)"`, `"delete node with two children (root)"` / `"(non-root)"`, `"delete black node with one red child (left)"` / `"(right, mirror)"`, `"delete root (single node tree)"`.
- Change needed: none — verify only.
- Verify with: `make test` (these cases already in `delete_cases[]`).

**Slice 1 — Case 5: sibling red (`rbtree.c:192–197`)**
- Situation: `x`'s sibling is red → rotate sibling up over parent, swap colors, sibling is now guaranteed black; loop re-enters.
- Mirror: `rbtree.c:218–223` (sib = `parent->left`, `rotate_right`).
- Existing tests: `"delete black leaf with red sibling"` / `"(mirror)"`.
- Change needed: none — verify only.
- Verify with: `make test`.

**Slice 2 — Case 4: sibling black, far nephew red (terminal) (`rbtree.c:202–213`)**
- Situation: sibling black with at least one red child; if the *near* nephew is red but far is black, rotate to convert to far-red first (`rbtree.c:203–208`), then terminal rotate+recolor at `rbtree.c:209–213`. Debt fully paid, no further climb.
- Mirror: `rbtree.c:228–239`.
- Existing tests: none directly named "Case 4" — currently only reached incidentally, if at all, inside the two-children/one-child cases. This is a **gap**: no table-driven case isolates "sibling black, red nephew, terminal rotation" (near-red-only-needs-conversion vs. far-red-already-good, both directions).
- Change needed: add table-driven cases for Case 4 (far-red direct, near-red-requiring-conversion) and their mirrors, if not already implicitly covered — need to hand-derive insertion sequences.
- Verify with: `make test` after adding; then `make asan` / `make memcheck` for the whole suite.

**Slice 3 — Case 3a: sibling black, both nephews black, parent red (terminal, `rbtree.c:198–201` + loop exit via `is_black(x)` false)**
- Situation: recolor sibling red, parent absorbs debt by turning black. One recolor pair, no rotation, no climb.
- Mirror: same code path (`rbtree.c:224–227`), direction-agnostic since it's a recolor, but should still confirm a right-sibling instance.
- Existing tests: not isolated as its own case currently — likely occurs as a sub-step inside other cases but not verified as the *terminal* outcome in a dedicated test.
- Change needed: add a table-driven case: black leaf, black sibling with two black children, red parent.
- Verify with: `make test`.

**Slice 4 — Case 3b: sibling black, both nephews black, parent black (climbs) — single-level and multi-level (`rbtree.c:198–201`, loop continues)**
- Situation: recolor sibling red, debt moves up to parent; loop re-runs with parent as new `x`. NOTES.md's documented gap: no table-driven test exercises climbing more than one level, nor a climb reaching the root and vanishing there.
- Mirror: `rbtree.c:224–227`, same climb logic.
- Existing tests: **none** — this is the explicit gap called out in NOTES.md line 105 and only covered by the fuzzer today.
- Change needed: add at least one table-driven case that forces a multi-level Case-3b climb (need a hand-verified insertion/deletion sequence, likely built the same way the existing "red sibling" case was — via an instrumented scratch check per the comment at `test_rbtree.c:334–337` — plus ideally one where the climb reaches the root and terminates by the loop's `parent != NULL` condition going false).
- Verify with: `make test`, then confirm via `rb_validate` in the new case; cross-check against `./build/fuzz 100000` since the fuzzer already stresses this path per NOTES.md's devlog.

**Slice 5 — full-suite regression check**
- After all table additions: `make test`, `make asan`, `make memcheck` (per CLAUDE.md's "done" bar) — zero findings required, matching the existing 2026-09-14 clean baseline.

### Scope note
No changes to `include/rbtree.h`, `src/rbtree.c`'s fixup logic (it already appears correct against the spec's decision tree — this plan is a coverage audit, not a rewrite), or unrelated milestones (`src/pool.c`, `tests/fault_alloc.c`). All proposed changes are additions to `delete_cases[]` in `tests/test_rbtree.c`, one table row (i.e., one slice) at a time.

Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

plan mapping each spec case to code and tests. Before approving, pushed on four specific claims
in that plan rather than accepting the slice boundaries as given.

- Claude's Slice 1 writeup said the Case-5 (red sibling) rotation causes the fixup "loop to
  re-enter." Asked for the actual control flow. Claude traced it and admitted the phrasing was
  imprecise: there is no `continue` or jump back to `while` after the Case-5 rotation — execution
  falls through, in the *same* iteration, into the Case-3/4 check now evaluated against the new
  (guaranteed-black) sibling. The loop only actually re-enters if that fall-through lands in
  Case 3b (parent black, debt climbs) and sets `x = parent`.

  whether near-red/far-black and far-red-directly are actually the same code path. They aren't:
  `rbtree.c`'s `else` branch has an inner `if (is_black(sib->right))` that only fires (and only
  then executes `rotate_right(t, sib)` to convert near-red into far-red) when the far nephew is
  black; the far-red-direct case skips that block entirely. Two distinct paths through the same
  branch, not one — Claude agreed and split Slice 2 into four sub-cases (2a/2b far-red-direct +
  mirror, 2c/2d near-red-conversion + mirror) instead of two.
- Asked why the plan asserted "no changes needed" for slices that already had passing tests, when
  passing tests (plus 10^5-op fuzz + asan/memcheck) aren't the same claim as "this specific named
  branch is deterministically pinned." Claude conceded the phrasing overclaimed and restated the
  actual scope: the algorithm's correctness evidence is the existing fuzz/asan/memcheck record: [[algorithm correctness comes from fuzz+asan+memcheck, not from unit tests alone]] the fuzzer's *aggregate* pass doesn't identify which named branch fired on any given op, so a

  could hide behind an otherwise-green fuzz run for a while. Tonight's work makes that
  explicit and per-case, not a claim that the algorithm was newly proven correct.

  black — is it inside the both-nephews-black branch, or elsewhere? Claude traced it: the
  both-nephews-black branch (`rbtree.c:198-201`) only recolors the sibling and reassigns
  `x = parent; parent = x->parent`. The actual recolor happens because the *next* `while`

unchanged (it was committed 2026-09-13, before this session); what changed was the plan's
*description* of that algorithm's control flow and the honesty of its "verified" claims. Working
agreement going forward: derive and hand-verify one slice's tree/insertion-sequence at a time,
walk through why it actually enters the named case (mirror included) before writing any test
code, and don't pre-derive later slices — exactly the mistake Episode 1 (mislabeled red-sibling
fixtures) already burned a turn on, this time caught before a fixture was even proposed.

content.text:
Good catch to double-check, but this isn't a bug — it's a common mix-up between two different things called "leaf."

The red-black invariants (`rb_validate`, `rbtree.c:340–369`) only require:

1. **The root is black** (invariant 1) — checked at `rbtree.c:341`. In both trees, the root (`d` in 2a, `e` in 2b) is black. ✓.
2. **No red node has a red child** (invariant 2) — checked at `rbtree.c:345` via `has_red_red`.

There's no invariant saying "every leaf must be black." The rule you're thinking of — "NIL leaves are black" — is real, but it's about the **conceptual NIL sentinel**, not about the last real key-bearing node before it. In this tree's design, `NULL` *is* NIL, and it's black by convention, enforced by `is_black()`:

```c
static bool is_red(const struct rb_node *n)  { return n != NULL && n->color == RED; }
static bool is_black(const struct rb_node *n) { return !is_red(n); }
```

`is_black(NULL)` returns `true` — a missing child is always treated as black, unconditionally, everywhere in the code (this is the exact thing CLAUDE.md calls out: "Every place that needs a node's color must route through a helper that treats `NULL` as black"). Same thing shows up in `black_height`:

```c
static int black_height(const struct rb_node *n) {
    if (n == NULL) return 1;   /* NIL contributes 1 by convention */
    ...
```

So `h` being red just means: `h` is a real node whose *own children* are both `NULL` (NIL, black). content.text:
## Slice 3 — Case 3a derived and verified

**Target:** first iteration of `delete_fixup` (`x=NULL`, i.e. a genuine deleted black leaf), sibling black with **both** children black (NIL or black), and — the part that took real searching — **parent red**. That last constraint turned out to be the hard part to construct by hand.

**Why this needed exhaustive search, not just hand-derivation:** I first tried to hand-build the obvious small shape (grandparent black, red parent `P` with two literal black-leaf children `x`/`S`) using 4–7 node trees, the same way I did for Slices 1–2. I wrote a brute-force check (compiling against the real `rb_insert`, not a re-implementation) over every insertion permutation of `n` sequential keys, searching for *any* tree containing a red non-root node with two black children whose own children are black. **Zero matches existed for n = 4 through 7.** Only at n = 8 did the pattern start appearing (3,456 of 40,320 permutations). ## Selected sequence: `a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h`, delete `a`

### Tree immediately before deletion

```
                    d(B)
                 /        \
              b(R)          f(R)
             /    \        /    \
          a(B)    c(B)   e(B)   g(B)
         /   \   /   \  /   \  /   \
       NIL  NIL NIL NIL NIL NIL NIL h(R)
                                    /   \
                                  NIL   NIL
```

- **`d`** — root, black (invariant 1).
- **`b`** — `d`'s left child, **red**.
- **`a`**, **`c`** — `b`'s children, both **black**, both leaves (all four grandchildren-slots are `NIL`).
- **`f`**, **`e`**, **`g`**, **`h`** — the right side of the tree, uninvolved in this deletion; included only because they must exist to keep black-heights equal on both sides of `d` (this is exactly why the search needed 8 nodes: `b`'s subtree alone, at only 3 nodes, can't be the whole tree — `d` needs a same-black-height sibling subtree, and `f`'s side is the smallest one the insertion sequence happens to produce).

### Answering each part

**The black leaf being deleted:** `a`. It's black, and both its children are `NIL` — this is the only shape that reaches the real fixup loop at all (`rb_delete`, `rbtree.c:265–274`: a node with a non-`NULL` child never calls `delete_fixup`; only a childless black node does).

**Its red parent:** `b`.

**Its black sibling:** `c` — `b`'s other child, black.

**Both nephews:** `c->left` and `c->right`. Both are `NIL`, which `is_black()` treats as black (`rbtree.c:28`, `is_black(NULL)` → true since `is_red(NULL)` is false). So "both nephews black" is satisfied trivially by `c` being a plain leaf — nephews don't need to be real black *nodes*, `NIL` already counts.

**`x` and `parent` when `delete_fixup` begins:** `rb_delete` first `transplant(t, n=a, child=NULL)` — this splices `NULL` into `a`'s old slot, so `b->left` is now `NULL`. Then, because `a` was black and had no child, it calls:
```c
delete_fixup(t, n->parent, NULL);   /* rbtree.c:273 */
```
So at entry: **`x = NULL`**, **`parent = b`**.

**Why the first iteration must enter Case 3a — not Case 5, Case 4, or the loop-exit shortcut:**

```c
while (parent != NULL && is_black(x)) {          /* parent=b (non-NULL), x=NULL (is_black(NULL)=true) -> loop runs */
    if (x == parent->left) {                      /* x=NULL, parent->left is now NULL (a was spliced out) -> true */
        struct rb_node *sib = parent->right;       /* sib = c */
        if (is_red(sib)) { ... }                    /* c is BLACK -> skip Case 5 */
        if (is_black(sib->left) && is_black(sib->right)) {  /* c->left=NIL, c->right=NIL, both black -> TRUE */
            sib->color = RED;                        /* Case 3: this branch, unconditionally reached */
            x = parent;
            parent = x->parent;
        }
```
Every gate that could have diverted control elsewhere fails to fire: `parent != NULL` (true, `b` exists) and `is_black(x)` (true, `x` is `NULL`) let the loop body run at all; `x == parent->left` is true because the transplant already left `NULL` in that slot; `sib` (`c`) is black, not red, so Case 5's rotation never triggers; and `c`'s two `NIL` children make the both-nephews-black test true, which is the *only* remaining branch (the `else` — Case 4 — is skipped entirely). There's no ambiguity or fallback path here: this tree was built specifically so every prior check fails and only Case 3 is left standing.

### The recoloring, and why the debt is absorbed here (not climbed further)

Inside the Case 3 branch: `sib->color = RED` — `c` turns red. `x = parent` — `x` becomes `b`. `parent = x->parent` — `parent` becomes `d`.

Back at the `while` guard: `parent` (`d`) is non-`NULL`, but `is_black(x)` now tests `is_black(b)`. `b` is **red**, so `is_black(b)` is `false` — the loop condition `parent != NULL && is_black(x)` is false, and the loop terminates immediately, without a second iteration. Falling out of the loop:
```c
if (x != NULL) x->color = BLACK;   /* rbtree.c:243 */
```
`x` is `b`, so `b` is painted black.

**Why this absorbs the debt instead of climbing:** the "extra black" that the vacated `a`-slot owed got moved, by the Case-3 recolor, from `c`'s branch (which lost a black node overall, since `c` went black→red) up onto the question of whether `b` itself can absorb one more black unit. Since `b` was red, it had "room" to become black without violating invariant 3 anywhere else — painting a red node black *adds* one black node to every path through it, exactly cancelling the one black node `a`'s deletion removed, and simultaneously fixing the fact that `c`'s branch now has one fewer black (from turning red) by counting `b` itself as the replacement black node both branches share. If `b` had been black instead of red, this same recolor would leave `b` still owing a black node to its own parent, and the loop would have to re-enter with `x=b`, `parent=d` — that's Case 3b, the climbing version, which is a separate slice. Here, because `b` happened to be red, the debt terminates in exactly one step: two recolors (`c`→red, `b`→black), zero rotations.

content.text:
## Your understanding, checked

You said the climb "switches all values to that current level's values and then checks again" — that's *directionally* right but let me be precise about what actually moves, using the real trace below, since "switches all values" undersells what's recomputed fresh each level.

The climbing branch does exactly two reassignments:
```c
sib->color = RED;
x = parent;              /* x becomes the OLD parent node */
parent = x->parent;      /* parent becomes the old parent's OWN parent (one level up) */
```
Only `x` and `parent` move. `sib` is **not** carried forward — it gets recomputed from scratch at the top of the next iteration (`sib = parent->right` or `parent->left`, whichever `x == parent->left` picks out), because the new `parent`'s sibling relationship has nothing to do with the previous level's `sib`. So "switches to that level's values" is right for `x`/`parent`, but the case-decision machinery (is `sib` red? are nephews black?) is re-run completely fresh each level, against a different node entirely one level up — it's not like the same case just repeats with relabeled pointers, each level can land in a genuinely different case (5, 3, or 4).

## What I found: multi-level climb — verified, but needed real search, not hand-derivation

Same story as Case 3a: I tried to hand-build a 2-level climb from small trees and couldn't. I instrumented a scratch copy of `delete_fixup` (compiled from the real code, with counters/logging added, never touching `src/rbtree.c`) to count loop iterations and log which case fires each level, then did randomized search over insertion orders, then delta-debugged (repeatedly tried removing one key at a time, keeping the removal only if the 3-iteration climb survived) down from 60 nodes to a **minimum of 38 nodes** for either direction — smaller sequences never produced a genuine 2-level climb no matter how I searched. This tracks with Case 3a's own finding: these deep-fixup shapes need real tree depth, they're not something a 5–8 node example can produce.

**Left-branch-starting climb** (38 keys, delete `"00027"`):
```
ITER 1: x=NIL      parent=00028(B)   CASE3        sib=00029(B), both nephews black -> CLIMB (parent black)
ITER 2: x=00028    parent=00026(B)   CASE3-mirror sib=00023(B), both nephews black -> CLIMB (parent black)
ITER 3: x=00026    parent=00021(R)   CASE4-mirror sib=00012(B), red nephew        -> TERMINAL
```
`rb_delete` → 0, `rb_validate` → 0 before and after, size 37. Two genuine Case-3b climbs (both ancestors along the path were black, so neither could absorb the debt — matches the trace from the previous slice, just now happening twice in a row instead of once), then a Case-4 terminal rotation ends it on the third level.

**Mirror-starting climb** (38 keys, delete `"059"`):
```
ITER 1: x=NIL   parent=058(B)  CASE3-mirror sib=057(B), both nephews black -> CLIMB (parent black)
ITER 2: x=058   parent=056(B)  CASE3-mirror sib=052(B), both nephews black -> CLIMB (parent black)
ITER 3: x=056   parent=048(R)  CASE4-mirror sib=040(B), red nephew         -> TERMINAL
```
Same shape, mirrored starting side. `rb_validate` clean before/after, size 37.

## What I could *not* find: a genuine climb-to-root

I specifically searched for this (random trees up to 500 nodes, plus a targeted search that finds the leaf whose *entire* ancestor chain up to the root is black — the best-case candidate for a full climb) and never got the debt to survive past 3 iterations, let alone reach the root. The reason, empirically: a root-to-leaf path with zero red ancestors is only achievable if all the "compensating" red nodes needed to keep black-heights balanced sit in the *sibling* branches near that path — which is exactly what produces a red nephew and triggers Case 4/5 termination early. This matches what NOTES.md itself already concluded ("We decided to extend the fuzzer to include case 3... where we need an extended fixup to climb up the tree" — not a hand-built table row). I'd propose **not** trying to force a table-driven climb-to-root case and instead relying on the fuzzer's existing 10^5-op coverage for that specific scenario, consistent with the project's own prior decision — unless you want me to keep searching further (e.g., much larger n, or a smarter construction via interleaved deletes rather than insert-only).

Fair — let me separate those claims properly instead of collapsing "I didn't find one" into "it can't happen."

## Longest verified climb: full iteration trace

Sequence (38 keys, ascending numeric labels `"00000"`–`"00058"`, insert order below), delete `"00027"`:

```
00030 00033 00058 00038 00034 00017 00031 00021 00018 00029 00028 00040 00027 00047
00026 00020 00006 00023 00012 00053 00000 00001 00056 00009 00054 00022 00015 00013
00002 00010 00008 00003 00024 00007 00005 00025 00016 00004
```

Ran against the real compiled `rb_delete`/`delete_fixup` (instrumented copy, logic untouched — I only added counters/`fprintf` around the existing branches, never changed a condition or assignment):

| Iter | `x` (entering) | `parent` | Branch taken | `sib` | Nephews | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `NIL` | `00028` (B) | `x==parent->left` → Case 3 | `00029` (B) | both `NIL`/black | `sib→RED`, `x=00028`, `parent=00026` — **climbs** |
| 2 | `00028` | `00026` (B) | mirror → Case 3 | `00023` (B) | both black | `sib→RED`, `x=00026`, `parent=00021` — **climbs** |
| 3 | `00026` | `00021` (R) | mirror → Case 4 | `00012` (B), red nephew | — | terminal rotate+recolor, **returns** |

`rb_validate` → 0 both before and after; `rb_delete` → 0; size 38→37. This is 2 genuine debt-climbing passes (both required `parent` to be black at that level, so nothing could absorb it locally) followed by a Case-4 termination on the third ancestor. I did not find any sequence — across every search strategy I tried, including the "all-ancestors-black" targeted search up to n=500 — that produced a 4th iteration or a `parent==NULL` exit. This is the longest I verified.

## Separating the three claims

**1. What's verified empirically:** exactly the table above, plus the earlier 60-node original (same shape, 3 iterations, never more) and the failed searches at n up to 500 using a search specifically biased toward the best-case setup (leaves reachable by an all-black ancestor chain). That's real evidence of *difficulty*, not of a ceiling.

**2. What follows from the RB invariants:** nothing in the five invariants (`rb_validate`'s checks, or the spec's Figure 1 rules) forbids a root-to-leaf path with zero red nodes. Invariant 3 only requires equal black-height across paths — a path of pure black nodes is legal as long as every other path agrees on the count, which can be satisfied by putting compensating red nodes in *other* branches. A fully-black perfect binary tree (every node black, root included) satisfies all five invariants trivially and would, if it existed, put the deletion of any leaf into a genuine climb that reaches the root's own recolor (harmlessly redundant, since the root's already black) — invariant 1 stays satisfied and the tree's black-height drops uniformly by one, which the spec explicitly allows ("black-height simply dropped by one uniformly, which is legal" — NOTES.md:178–181). So **the invariants themselves don't rule out climb-to-root** — if anything they explicitly anticipate it.

**3. What remains unproven either way:** whether `rb_insert`'s specific fixup algorithm, starting from empty and using only sequential inserts, can ever reach a state with an entirely-black root-to-leaf path *and* matching black-both-children siblings at every level along it. My search intuition (red nodes get pushed into sibling branches to balance black-height, which tends to produce a red nephew that terminates the climb early) is a plausible mechanism for why it's *hard*, but I have not proven it's *impossible* — I sampled a vanishingly small fraction of the possible insertion orders even at n=500 (500! is astronomically larger than any trial count), and I didn't try more targeted constructions (e.g., explicitly simulating the B-tree-node-split correspondence that produces all-black regions, or building the tree via interleaved insert/delete rather than insert-only). This is a genuinely open question given the search I've done, not a settled negative result.

## Does the spec require a dedicated climb-to-root table case?

No. Re-reading the actual grading requirement (NOTES.md:58–60): *"table-driven tests for rb_delete covering, at minimum: a red leaf, a black leaf with a red sibling, a node with two children, and deletion of the root."* That's the full explicit list — it does not name Case 3b, a multi-level climb, or climb-to-root. The multi-level-climb gap comes from a different part of the file: the **"Confusions"** section (NOTES.md:105), which is the project author's own working note, not spec text — and it explicitly resolves the gap by extending the *fuzzer*, not by adding a 10th table row: *"We decided to extend the fuzzer to include case 3, where we need an extended fixup to climb up the tree."* `tests/fuzz.c` already runs ≥10^5 ops with `rb_validate` every 100 ops, which is the mechanism this project already chose for stress-covering exactly this scenario probabilistically over many random trees — a better fit than a hand-built row for a case that (per the evidence above) needs real depth and isn't easy to pin down deterministically.

So: the two verified multi-level-climb cases (left-start and mirror-start, both genuinely exercising 2 real Case-3b climbs) are legitimate *additional* coverage worth adding, since they directly address NOTES.md's named gap ("did not exercise a multi-level delete_fixup climb"). A dedicated climb-to-root table row is not required by the spec, and given the evidence above I'd defer it to the fuzzer rather than force a 500+ node fixture into the test table — but that's a scope call, not a settled fact, and if you want to keep searching for one I'm glad to continue rather than close it out.

1	# CLAUDE.md
2	
3	This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.
4	
5	## Project status
6	
7	This is a CS370 lab implementing a red-black tree in C. `include/rbtree.h` is the frozen
8	contract. `NOTES.md` contains the assignment spec, the design decisions already made
9	(including a devlog of the NIL/parent-pointer/teardown reasoning), and constraints that must
10	not be violated — read it before writing any code here.
11	
12	Current state of `src/rbtree.c`: `rb_create`, the node/tree structs (with parent pointer),
13	the `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` seam, `rb_find` (real BST search), `rb_size`, `rb_insert` (with
14	rotations and insertion fixup, all cases + mirrors), `rb_foreach` (recursive in-order),
15	`rb_validate` (all five invariants), and `rb_destroy` are implemented. `rb_destroy` already
16	uses the non-recursive "Reach" technique (rotate into a right spine while freeing) — see
17	"The Reach" below; it is not just the ungraded future work it's described as there.
18	**`rb_delete` is now implemented**, including `delete_fixup` (the doubly-black fixup loop,
19	all cases plus the mirrored right-child symmetry) — both live in `src/rbtree.c` as of the
20	M2 commits (`f32e9ef`..`8c55919`). `src/pool.c` and `tests/fault_alloc.c` remain empty —
21	out of scope until their respective milestones/mutations.
22	
23	`tests/fuzz.c` runs insert/find/delete ops against a reference-model oracle (an array of
24	key/value pairs), interleaving `rb_delete` per its later M2 commit. `tests/test_rbtree.c`
25	covers insert/find (including overwrite and missing-key cases), foreach ordering, validate
26	(ascending/descending/scrambled/empty), the insertion-fixup rotation cases (LL/RR/LR/RL,
27	red-uncle recolor), destroy (single node, chain, value_free-once), and now the table-driven
28	`rb_delete` cases required by the spec (red leaf + mirror, black leaf with red sibling +
29	mirror, two-children root/non-root, single-node root, black node with one red child +
30	mirror), plus missing-key delete and value_free-on-delete checks.
31	
32	As of 2026-09-14: `make test`, `make asan`, and `make memcheck` (from a clean rebuild) all
33	pass with zero findings, including the fuzzer at 10^5 ops (asan/test) and 2×10^4 ops
34	(memcheck, per the Makefile's smaller valgrind op count).
35	
36	## Build and test commands
37	
38	```sh
39	make          # builds build/test_rbtree and build/fuzz
40	make test     # builds, then runs ./build/test_rbtree && ./build/fuzz 100000
41	make asan     # rebuilds with -fsanitize=address,undefined, then runs `test`
42	make memcheck # builds, then runs both binaries under valgrind --leak-check=full
43	              # (test_rbtree, and fuzz with 20000 ops), --error-exitcode=1
44	make clean
45	```
46	
47	There is no test filter — `test_rbtree` is a single binary of unit tests (including the
48	table-driven `rb_delete` cases) run via `./build/test_rbtree`; the fuzzer takes an operation
49	count as argv[1] (`./build/fuzz 100000`). Toolchain is `gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror`.
50	Every change must be clean under both `make asan` and `make memcheck` before it's considered
51	done — the spec requires zero findings across the whole suite, including the empty-tree case.
52	
53	## Architecture (per NOTES.md / include/rbtree.h)
54	
55	- **Ownership contract**: keys are C strings, always copied and owned by the tree. Values
56	  are opaque `void *`; the tree takes ownership of a value only on a *successful* `rb_insert`
57	  and releases it via the `value_free` destructor (from `rb_create`) on delete/destroy/overwrite.
58	  On insert failure the tree is unchanged and the caller keeps ownership of `value`. Overwriting
59	  an existing key frees the old value (the tree is its sole owner at that instant) before
60	  installing the new one. Every allocation has exactly one owner at all times.
61	- **Allocation seam**: all allocation in `src/rbtree.c` routes through two 4-line wrappers,
62	  `rb_malloc`/`rb_free`, which just forward to `malloc`/`free`. This is the optional tip from
63	  the spec (not a hard requirement) — it pays off in the next assignment, where a test harness
64	  makes allocation fail on demand.
65	- **Node shape**: nodes carry a parent pointer (a deliberate design choice beyond the bare
66	  minimum). NIL is represented as `NULL`, not a shared sentinel object — a shared sentinel
67	  is incompatible with per-node parent pointers (every node with a missing child would claim
68	  to be that one sentinel's parent). Every place that needs a node's color must route through
69	  a helper that treats `NULL` as black, never dereference `->color` on a pointer that might
70	  be `NULL`. Full reasoning in NOTES.md's devlog. Current, actual shape (matches
71	  `src/rbtree.c`):
72	  ```c
73	  typedef enum { RED, BLACK } rb_color_t;
74	  struct rb_node {
75	      char           *key;    /* heap copy; the tree owns it */
76	      void           *value;  /* ownership per the header contract */
77	      struct rb_node *parent; /* NULL for the root */
78	      struct rb_node *left;
79	      struct rb_node *right;
80	      rb_color_t      color;
81	  };
82	  ```
83	
84	- **Rotations own root maintenance**: `rb_validate` must never be responsible for fixing up
85	  `t->root` — rotations themselves must keep it correct.
86	- **Deletion fixup**: implement all cases, including deleting a black node with exactly one
87	  child, and the mirrored (right-child-of-right-child) symmetry of every fixup case — the
88	  spec explicitly calls out the mirror image as "the half people forget."
89	- **`rb_foreach` / `rb_destroy`**: recursion is permitted for this assignment (spec §9). See
90	  "The Reach" below for the ungraded non-recursive teardown.
91	- **`rb_validate` invariants** (must detect and report *which* invariant broke):
92	  1. root is black
93	  2. no red node has a red child
94	  3. every root-to-NIL path has the same black-height
95	  4. in-order traversal is strictly increasing under `strcmp`
96	  5. `rb_size` matches the actual node count
97	- **Test coverage requirements**: table-driven `rb_delete` tests covering at minimum a red
98	  leaf, a black leaf with a red sibling, a node with two children, and root deletion — each
99	  asserting `rb_validate` and `rb_size` afterward. The fuzzer (`tests/fuzz.c`) must run ≥ 10^5
100	  random insert/find/delete ops against a reference model (sorted array or linked list is
101	  fine), calling `rb_validate` at least every 100 ops, and must be clean under both asan and
102	  memcheck.
103	
104	## The Reach (ungraded)
105	
106	Non-recursive, O(1)-auxiliary-space teardown is **not required** for this assignment — it carries
107	no points (spec §10, "The Reach"). Recursion in `rb_foreach`/`rb_destroy` is explicitly permitted

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project status

This is a CS370 lab implementing a red-black tree in C. `include/rbtree.h` is the frozen
contract. `NOTES.md` contains the assignment spec, the design decisions already made
(including a devlog of the NIL/parent-pointer/teardown reasoning), and constraints that must
not be violated — read it before writing any code here.

Current state of `src/rbtree.c`: `rb_create`, the node/tree structs (with parent pointer),
the `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` seam, `rb_find` (real BST search), `rb_size`, `rb_insert` (with
rotations and insertion fixup, all cases + mirrors), `rb_foreach` (recursive in-order),
`rb_validate` (all five invariants), and `rb_destroy` are implemented. `rb_destroy` already
uses the non-recursive "Reach" technique (rotate into a right spine while freeing) — see
"The Reach" below; it is not just the ungraded future work it's described as there.
**`rb_delete` is now implemented**, including `delete_fixup` (the doubly-black fixup loop,
all cases plus the mirrored right-child symmetry) — both live in `src/rbtree.c` as of the
M2 commits (`f32e9ef`..`8c55919`). `src/pool.c` and `tests/fault_alloc.c` remain empty —
out of scope until their respective milestones/mutations.

`tests/fuzz.c` runs insert/find/delete ops against a reference-model oracle (an array of
key/value pairs), interleaving `rb_delete` per its later M2 commit. `tests/test_rbtree.c`
covers insert/find (including overwrite and missing-key cases), foreach ordering, validate
(ascending/descending/scrambled/empty), the insertion-fixup rotation cases (LL/RR/LR/RL,
red-uncle recolor), destroy (single node, chain, value_free-once), and now the table-driven
`rb_delete` cases required by the spec (red leaf + mirror, black leaf with red sibling +
mirror, two-children root/non-root, single-node root, black node with one red child +
mirror), plus missing-key delete and value_free-on-delete checks.

As of 2026-09-14: `make test`, `make asan`, and `make memcheck` (from a clean rebuild) all
pass with zero findings, including the fuzzer at 10^5 ops (asan/test) and 2×10^4 ops
(memcheck, per the Makefile's smaller valgrind op count).

## Build and test commands

```sh
make          # builds build/test_rbtree and build/fuzz
make test     # builds, then runs ./build/test_rbtree && ./build/fuzz 100000
make asan     # rebuilds with -fsanitize=address,undefined, then runs `test`
make memcheck # builds, then runs both binaries under valgrind --leak-check=full
              # (test_rbtree, and fuzz with 20000 ops), --error-exitcode=1
make clean
```

There is no test filter — `test_rbtree` is a single binary of unit tests (including the
table-driven `rb_delete` cases) run via `./build/test_rbtree`; the fuzzer takes an operation
count as argv[1] (`./build/fuzz 100000`). Toolchain is `gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror`.
Every change must be clean under both `make asan` and `make memcheck` before it's considered
done — the spec requires zero findings across the whole suite, including the empty-tree case.

## Architecture (per NOTES.md / include/rbtree.h)

- **Ownership contract**: keys are C strings, always copied and owned by the tree. Values
  are opaque `void *`; the tree takes ownership of a value only on a *successful* `rb_insert`
  and releases it via the `value_free` destructor (from `rb_create`) on delete/destroy/overwrite.
  On insert failure the tree is unchanged and the caller keeps ownership of `value`. Overwriting
  an existing key frees the old value (the tree is its sole owner at that instant) before
  installing the new one. Every allocation has exactly one owner at all times.
- **Allocation seam**: all allocation in `src/rbtree.c` routes through two 4-line wrappers,
  `rb_malloc`/`rb_free`, which just forward to `malloc`/`free`. This is the optional tip from
  the spec (not a hard requirement) — it pays off in the next assignment, where a test harness
  makes allocation fail on demand.
- **Node shape**: nodes carry a parent pointer (a deliberate design choice beyond the bare
  minimum). NIL is represented as `NULL`, not a shared sentinel object — a shared sentinel
  is incompatible with per-node parent pointers (every node with a missing child would claim
  to be that one sentinel's parent). Every place that needs a node's color must route through
  a helper that treats `NULL` as black, never dereference `->color` on a pointer that might
  be `NULL`. Full reasoning in NOTES.md's devlog. Current, actual shape (matches
  `src/rbtree.c`):
  ```c
  typedef enum { RED, BLACK } rb_color_t;
  struct rb_node {
      char           *key;    /* heap copy; the tree owns it */
      void           *value;  /* ownership per the header contract */
      struct rb_node *parent; /* NULL for the root */
      struct rb_node *left;
      struct rb_node *right;
      rb_color_t      color;
  };
  ```

- **Rotations own root maintenance**: `rb_validate` must never be responsible for fixing up
  `t->root` — rotations themselves must keep it correct.
- **Deletion fixup**: implement all cases, including deleting a black node with exactly one
  child, and the mirrored (right-child-of-right-child) symmetry of every fixup case — the
  spec explicitly calls out the mirror image as "the half people forget."
- **`rb_foreach` / `rb_destroy`**: recursion is permitted for this assignment (spec §9). See
  "The Reach" below for the ungraded non-recursive teardown.
- **`rb_validate` invariants** (must detect and report *which* invariant broke):
  1. root is black
  2. no red node has a red child
  3. every root-to-NIL path has the same black-height
  4. in-order traversal is strictly increasing under `strcmp`
  5. `rb_size` matches the actual node count
- **Test coverage requirements**: table-driven `rb_delete` tests covering at minimum a red
  leaf, a black leaf with a red sibling, a node with two children, and root deletion — each
  asserting `rb_validate` and `rb_size` afterward. The fuzzer (`tests/fuzz.c`) must run ≥ 10^5
  random insert/find/delete ops against a reference model (sorted array or linked list is
  fine), calling `rb_validate` at least every 100 ops, and must be clean under both asan and
  memcheck.

## The Reach (ungraded)

Non-recursive, O(1)-auxiliary-space teardown is **not required** for this assignment — it carries
no points (spec §10, "The Reach"). Recursion in `rb_foreach`/`rb_destroy` is explicitly permitted
here (spec §9); the non-recursive constraint is a preview of the *next* assignment's stack-budget
requirements, not something this milestone set is graded on. If time allows, the technique is to
rotate into a right spine while freeing so the tree's own pointer fields serve as the bookkeeping,
implemented behind a second function and checked against the fuzzer's teardown — see CS370-HW1.pdf
§10 for the full writeup before attempting it.

## Process requirements / deliverables (spec §7, §15, §17)

These are graded independently of the code and must not be neglected or bulk-generated at the end:

- **Git history**: ≥ 8 meaningful commits tracking the milestones (M0–M3 in the schedule table,
  spec §5 — `M<n>: <what>` in a commit message names the milestone, not a "Mutation"). A single
  "final submission" commit is an automatic process-grade of zero.
- **`PROMPTLOG.md`**: 4–6 annotated episodes (prompt, what came back, your judgment — accepted,
  rejected, or pushed back on, and why). Must include at least: one plan you revised, one
  rejected/oversized diff, one tool-output debugging loop (e.g. a valgrind/asan trace fed back
  verbatim), and one adversarial-review finding you triaged. Raw transcript pastes score nothing —
  the annotation is the deliverable.
- **`REFLECTION.md`** (~1 page): where the agent was most/least reliable, one bug it introduced
  that you caught and how, and what most surprised you as a C newcomer.
- **Raw session transcripts**: the actual `.jsonl` files under `~/.claude/projects/<project>/`,
  copied in as-is — not a summary, not `/export`, not retyped. Work in this project's own
  dedicated directory so the copy is a single `cp` and doesn't pull in unrelated sessions.
  Transcripts auto-purge after 30 days by default — copy them out periodically.
- Grading corroborates these against the repo (commits, diffs, test files, line numbers), not
  against the log's own narrative — a claim with no matching artifact doesn't count.

## Working style noted in NOTES.md

# rbtree-lab: project rules
## Commands
- Build & unit tests: ‘make test‘
- Sanitizers: ‘make asan‘ Valgrind: ‘make memcheck‘
- A change is DONE only when all three pass. Always run them; show output.
## Hard constraints
- NEVER modify include/rbtree.h. It is the graded contract.
- Check every allocation. malloc can return NULL; a NULL return must
leave the tree unchanged and return the documented error code.
- NEVER weaken, skip, or delete a test to make the suite pass. If a test
looks wrong, stop and explain why instead.
## Style
- C23. -Wall -Wextra -Werror must stay clean. No VLAs.
- Error handling: goto-cleanup pattern for multi-allocation functions.
- Prefer the smallest diff that passes. Do not refactor unrelated code.
- Every non-obvious loop gets a one-line invariant comment.
## Workflow
- For any multi-file or algorithmic change: propose a plan and wait for
approval before editing.
- Commit only from a green state; message format "M<n>: <what>".


Plan first, keep diffs small, verify everything with the build tools above, and don't merge
anything that can't be explained.

  the spec (not a hard requirement) — it pays off in the next assignment, where a test harness
  makes allocation fail on demand.
- **Node shape**: nodes carry a parent pointer (a deliberate design choice beyond the bare
  minimum). NIL is represented as `NULL`, not a shared sentinel object — a shared sentinel
  is incompatible with per-node parent pointers (every node with a missing child would claim
  to be that one sentinel's parent). Every place that needs a node's color must route through
  a helper that treats `NULL` as black, never dereference `->color` on a pointer that might
  be `NULL`. Full reasoning in NOTES.md's devlog. Current, actual shape (matches
  `src/rbtree.c`):
  ```c
  typedef enum { RED, BLACK } rb_color_t;
  struct rb_node {
      char           *key;    /* heap copy; the tree owns it */
      void           *value;  /* ownership per the header contract */
      struct rb_node *parent; /* NULL for the root */
      struct rb_node *left;
      struct rb_node *right;
      rb_color_t      color;
  };
  ```

- **Rotations own root maintenance**: `rb_validate` must never be responsible for fixing up
  `t->root` — rotations themselves must keep it correct.
- **Deletion fixup**: implement all cases, including deleting a black node with exactly one
  child, and the mirrored (right-child-of-right-child) symmetry of every fixup case — the
  spec explicitly calls out the mirror image as "the half people forget."
- **`rb_foreach` / `rb_destroy`**: recursion is permitted for this assignment (spec §9). See
  "The Reach" below for the ungraded non-recursive teardown.
- **`rb_validate` invariants** (must detect and report *which* invariant broke):
  1. root is black
  2. no red node has a red child
  3. every root-to-NIL path has the same black-height
  4. in-order traversal is strictly increasing under `strcmp`
  5. `rb_size` matches the actual node count
- **Test coverage requirements**: table-driven `rb_delete` tests covering at minimum a red
  leaf, a black leaf with a red sibling, a node with two children, and root deletion — each
  asserting `rb_validate` and `rb_size` afterward. The fuzzer (`tests/fuzz.c`) must run ≥ 10^5
  random insert/find/delete ops against a reference model (sorted array or linked list is
  fine), calling `rb_validate` at least every 100 ops, and must be clean under both asan and
  memcheck.

## The Reach (ungraded)

Non-recursive, O(1)-auxiliary-space teardown is **not required** for this assignment — it carries
no points (spec §10, "The Reach"). Recursion in `rb_foreach`/`rb_destroy` is explicitly permitted
here (spec §9); the non-recursive constraint is a preview of the *next* assignment's stack-budget
requirements, not something this milestone set is graded on. If time allows, the technique is to
rotate into a right spine while freeing so the tree's own pointer fields serve as the bookkeeping,
implemented behind a second function and checked against the fuzzer's teardown — see CS370-HW1.pdf
§10 for the full writeup before attempting it.

## Process requirements / deliverables (spec §7, §15, §17)

These are graded independently of the code and must not be neglected or bulk-generated at the end:

- **Git history**: ≥ 8 meaningful commits tracking the milestones (M0–M3 in the schedule table,
  spec §5 — `M<n>: <what>` in a commit message names the milestone, not a "Mutation"). A single
  "final submission" commit is an automatic process-grade of zero.
- **`PROMPTLOG.md`**: 4–6 annotated episodes (prompt, what came back, your judgment — accepted,
  rejected, or pushed back on, and why). Must include at least: one plan you revised, one
  rejected/oversized diff, one tool-output debugging loop (e.g. a valgrind/asan trace fed back
  verbatim), and one adversarial-review finding you triaged. Raw transcript pastes score nothing —
  the annotation is the deliverable.
- **`REFLECTION.md`** (~1 page): where the agent was most/least reliable, one bug it introduced
  that you caught and how, and what most surprised you as a C newcomer.
- **Raw session transcripts**: the actual `.jsonl` files under `~/.claude/projects/<project>/`,
  copied in as-is — not a summary, not `/export`, not retyped. Work in this project's own
  dedicated directory so the copy is a single `cp` and doesn't pull in unrelated sessions.
  Transcripts auto-purge after 30 days by default — copy them out periodically.
- Grading corroborates these against the repo (commits, diffs, test files, line numbers), not
  against the log's own narrative — a claim with no matching artifact doesn't count.

CC := gcc
CFLAGS := -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Iinclude
SRC := src/rbtree.c
TSRC := tests/test_rbtree.c
BIN := build/test_rbtree
FUZZBIN := build/fuzz

all: $(BIN) $(FUZZBIN)

$(BIN): $(SRC) $(TSRC) include/rbtree.h
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SRC) $(TSRC) -o $@

$(FUZZBIN): $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c include/rbtree.h
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c -o $@

test: $(BIN) $(FUZZBIN)
	./$(BIN) && ./$(FUZZBIN) 100000

asan: CFLAGS += -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer
asan: clean test

memcheck: all
	valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all \
		--error-exitcode=1 ./$(BIN)
	valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all \
		--error-exitcode=1 ./$(FUZZBIN) 20000
clean:
	rm -rf build

.PHONY: all test asan memcheck clean

## Exact commands used (fixed seed: `42`)

**ASan+UBSan build (manual compile, not via `make asan` since that target rebuilds with a time-based seed):**
```sh
gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Iinclude -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer src/rbtree.c tests/fuzz.c -o build/fuzz_asan
./build/fuzz_asan 100000 42
```
Output:
```
fuzz: seed=42 op_count=100000
fuzz: 100000 insert/find/delete ops OK
```

**Valgrind memcheck (plain, non-sanitized build — sanitizer + valgrind conflict is the exact issue already documented in PROMPTLOG.md episode 3):**
```sh
gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Iinclude src/rbtree.c tests/fuzz.c -o build/fuzz
valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all --error-exitcode=1 ./build/fuzz 100000 42
```

```

fuzz: 100000 insert/find/delete ops OK

```

Both invoke `./build/fuzz[_asan] 100000 42` — `argv[1]`=op count, `argv[2]`=seed (`tests/fuzz.c:79-80`), so the two runs traverse the identical operation sequence. `rb_validate` fires at `op % 100 == 0` (`tests/fuzz.c:152`), i.e. 1,000 times per run.
